title: Zoning & cleaning the surgery between patients
blurb: Clean and contaminated zones, keeping gloved hands out of clean storage, the between-patient clear-down, and colour-coded cleaning equipment.
question: Halfway through a filling, the dentist asks for a matrix band that isn't on the tray. You're wearing contaminated gloves and the bands are in a drawer under the worktop. How do you get one without spreading contamination, and how will you clean the surgery before the next patient?

teach.h: Zoning: keeping contamination in its place
teach.body: Zoning means dividing the surgery into a contaminated (dirty) zone and a clean zone. The contaminated zone is everything within reach during treatment: the chair, light, bracket table, spittoon and the worktop where the tray sits. It is reached by spatter, aerosol and gloved hands. The clean zone is drawers, cupboards, stock, the computer and paperwork, and only clean hands go there. Keeping them apart stops one patient's micro-organisms travelling to the next.

teach.h: Plan ahead so you never reach into clean storage
teach.body: Set out everything you are likely to need before treatment starts, so you don't have to open drawers mid-procedure. If something extra is needed, don't reach in with contaminated gloves: take your gloves off and clean your hands, or ask a colleague with clean hands to fetch it. Once you've touched a drawer handle or stock with dirty gloves, the clean zone is contaminated. The same applies in decontamination: change heavy-duty gloves before touching a clean worktop.

head: When
What
rows: Chair, light handle, bracket table, spittoon, worktop in the zone, barriers
Suction lines with the practice's aspirator cleaner; spittoon; all work surfaces
Clinical floor and fixtures, following the cleaning schedule
teach.caption: Clinical floors should be sealed and impervious, never carpeted, so they can be cleaned properly. Uncluttered worktops are quicker to clean well.
This is the colour scheme HTM 01-05 suggests for dental practices (hospitals use yellow for isolation rooms). Mops, buckets and cloths never move between areas.

teach.body: A mop used in the toilets and then in the surgery carries micro-organisms between them, and so does one used in the surgery and then in the staff kitchen. Colour coding makes it obvious which mops, buckets and cloths belong where, so anyone, including contract cleaners, can see at a glance if equipment is in the wrong place. Store each set separately, clean and dry.

teach.text: A sealed pouch or a closed drawer is not 'safe' from dirty gloves. Touching the outside contaminates it for the next person. Remove gloves and clean your hands, or ask a colleague with clean hands.

items: The contaminated zone is everything within reach during treatment; the clean zone is storage, stock and records.
Never reach into clean drawers or cupboards with contaminated gloves.
Clear down between patients: sharps, instruments, waste, flush, clean clean-to-dirty, barriers, PPE off.
Change heavy-duty gloves before touching clean worktops in decontamination.
Colour-coded cleaning equipment stays in its own area.

summary: You can now divide the surgery into clean and contaminated zones, keep contaminated gloves out of clean storage, clear down and clean the surgery between patients in a logical order, and explain why cleaning equipment is colour-coded.

A.q: During treatment, a nurse wearing contaminated gloves opens a drawer to get clean bibs. Which principle has she broken?
A.why: Touching clean storage with contaminated gloves breaks the separation of clean and contaminated zones.

whyNot.0: No instrument has been reused here.
whyNot.1: She hasn't removed any PPE, so doffing order isn't the issue.

A.q: A cleaner uses the same mop in the surgery and the staff kitchen. Why should cleaning equipment be colour-coded?
options: To stop equipment moving between areas
To make the cupboard look tidy
So cleaners know which mops to reorder
A.why: Colour coding keeps each set of equipment in its own area, preventing cross-contamination between them.

whyNot.1: Tidiness is a side effect, not the purpose.
whyNot.2: Colour doesn't change how long a mop lasts.
whyNot.3: Purchasing isn't the reason; infection control is.

A.q: What is the main purpose of zoning in the dental surgery?
options: To keep contamination in one area
To reduce the need for PPE
To store more stock in the surgery
A.why: Zoning confines contamination to the treatment area so it can be cleaned, and keeps storage and records clean.

whyNot.0: Good organisation may save time, but the purpose is infection control.
whyNot.2: PPE is still needed; zoning works alongside it.

B.q: A nurse has been scrubbing instruments in heavy-duty gloves and now needs to wipe a clean worktop. What should she do first?
options: Rinse the gloves under the tap
Carry on with the same gloves
Use alcohol gel on the gloves
B.why: Gloves used on dirty instruments must be changed (or decontaminated as the protocol says) before touching a clean area.

whyNot.0: A quick rinse doesn't make dirty gloves safe for clean surfaces.
whyNot.1: Using the same gloves carries contamination onto the clean worktop.
whyNot.2: Alcohol gel isn't a way of decontaminating gloves.

B.q: When cleaning the surgery between patients, which approach is correct?
options: Work from clean to dirty areas
Wipe in circles with one cloth
B.why: Working from cleaner to dirtier areas avoids spreading contamination onto surfaces you've already cleaned.

whyNot.0: Dry dusting stirs dust into the air; surfaces are cleaned with damp detergent or disinfectant wipes.
whyNot.2: Circling with one cloth spreads contamination around; use fresh wipes.
whyNot.3: Spatter and aerosol contaminate surfaces you can't see, so the whole zone is cleaned.

B.q: Why are barriers such as cling film put over the light handles and chair controls?
options: They're touched often and hard to clean
They make the controls easier to use
They are required by the GDC
B.why: Barriers protect items that are touched frequently but are awkward to clean, and are replaced between patients.

whyNot.1: Barriers don't affect the light's temperature.
whyNot.2: They don't make controls easier to use.
whyNot.3: The GDC doesn't specify barriers; they're part of practice infection control.

C.q: Halfway through a filling, the dentist asks for a material that isn't on the tray. What is the best way to get it without breaking zoning?
options: Remove gloves, clean hands, then fetch it
Open the drawer with gloved fingertips
Ask the patient to pass it to you
Open the cupboard with your elbow
C.why: Removing gloves and cleaning your hands (or asking a colleague with clean hands) keeps the clean zone clean.

whyNot.1: Even fingertips of a contaminated glove contaminate the drawer.
whyNot.3: Your elbow and sleeve can carry contamination, and you'd still touch the stock with dirty gloves.

C.q: Which of these belongs to the clean zone of the surgery?
C.why: Stock in drawers and cupboards is clean storage, touched only with clean hands.

whyNot.0: The bracket table is within reach during treatment, so it's contaminated.
whyNot.1: The spittoon is in the contaminated zone.

C.q: Which floor covering is suitable for a clinical dental surgery?
C.why: Clinical floors must be sealed and impervious so spills can be cleaned and disinfected properly.

whyNot.0: Carpet can't be cleaned properly after spills.
whyNot.1: Rugs trap dirt and are a trip hazard.
whyNot.3: Untreated wood absorbs fluids and can't be disinfected.

reteach.title: Kitchen rules for the surgery
reteach.question: When you cook with raw chicken, you don't open the fridge or the cutlery drawer with chicken on your hands. How does that help you understand zoning?

blocks.body: A careful cook keeps a 'raw' area on the chopping board and a 'clean' area for everything else. Before touching the fridge door or cutlery drawer, they wash their hands, because otherwise the next person to open the drawer picks up the germs. Your contaminated gloves are raw chicken hands. The treatment area is the chopping board; drawers, stock and the keyboard are the fridge and cutlery drawer.

blocks.h: Need something from a drawer mid-treatment?

children.label: Don't touch the drawer
children.sub: Remove gloves and clean hands, or ask a colleague

blocks.text: Cleaning order matters too: clean to dirty, top to bottom, with fresh wipes, so you don't spread contamination onto surfaces you've already cleaned.

explain.body: The contaminated zone is within reach during treatment: chair, light, bracket table, spittoon, the worktop under the tray. The clean zone is storage, stock and records.

test.q: Which of these is part of the contaminated zone during treatment?
test.why: The bracket table is within reach during treatment and is contaminated by gloved hands and spatter.

whyNot.2: The clean instrument cupboard is in the clean zone.
whyNot.3: Reception is outside the clinical area altogether.

explain.body: Contaminated gloves never touch clean drawers, cupboards, pouches or worktops. Remove gloves and clean your hands first, or ask a colleague with clean hands.

test.q: A nurse wearing contaminated gloves opens a cupboard of sterile instrument pouches. What has happened?
options: Nothing, as the pouches are sealed
test.why: The cupboard and the outside of the pouches are now contaminated, breaking the separation of clean and dirty zones.

whyNot.0: The outsides of the pouches are contaminated and will be handled later.
whyNot.1: No PPE was removed, so doffing order isn't involved.
whyNot.3: Touching pouches doesn't sterilise them; it contaminates them.

explain.body: Sharps safe, instruments into a lidded box, waste into the right streams, flush and aspirate, clean the zone from clean to dirty, change barriers, then remove PPE and clean your hands.

test.q: What should be done first when clearing the surgery after a patient?
options: Make sure all sharps are safely disposed
Lay out the next patient's tray
Take off your PPE and clean your hands
Wipe down the chair with disinfectant spray
test.why: Sharps are made safe first so nobody is injured while clearing the rest of the surgery.

whyNot.1: Setting up comes last, once the surgery is clean.
whyNot.2: PPE stays on until cleaning is finished.
whyNot.3: Surfaces are cleaned after sharps, instruments and waste are cleared.

explain.body: Mops, buckets and cloths are colour-coded so each set stays in its own area, such as toilets, kitchen or clinical rooms, and never carries contamination between them.

test.q: What is the main reason for colour-coded mops and cloths?
options: Showing which cleaner did the job
test.why: Colour coding stops equipment being used in more than one area, preventing cross-contamination.

whyNot.0: Branding is irrelevant to infection control.
whyNot.2: Colour shows the area, not the person.
